<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with disciplined, closed-book reasoning and no fake sourcing. CON's best route was the word "achievable": no signatories, 700,000 settlers, the Gaza 8,000-vs-scaling-up-eighty-fold comparison, and the sharp claim that the two-state frame has become the alibi that makes annexation deniable. That created genuine pressure, and CON also landed a clean hit on PRO's vague falsifier ("outgrows what compensation can absorb"). But PRO controlled the decisive comparative frame the motion actually sets: "least-bad achievable" is inherently a comparison, and PRO held CON's own preferred trajectory to the same standard. PRO's "single door" argument — that incremental rights inside one polity still terminates in a national majority accepting minority status, an ask at least as large as a border, obtainable only through the same door and requiring more pressure — was never fully closed. CON's reply (a single simultaneous act versus cheap, unsignable increments) is clever, but it effectively converts CON's case from an achievable outcome into an ongoing process, which PRO named accurately in closing. PRO also turned CON's Q2 mechanism damagingly: the "collapse of temporariness" route requires formal annexation to occur first and then hope the world prices it, which is a poor answer on a least-bad metric; CON's denial ("I never welcomed permanent hierarchy") was rhetorically strong but did not dismantle the mechanism critique. PRO's early reframe that the motion asks about a long-term destination also blunted CON's insistence on a currently existing signatory coalition. Both sides had clipped turns (CON twice), a small execution cost. Narrow but real edge to PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's symmetry turn on the settlers and the "door": if armed Hebron settlers rejecting Palestinian sovereignty sinks a border, they equally sink one-state equality — except there they sit inside the legislature, and whatever pressure could extract minority status from a national majority could buy a border far more cheaply. CON's asymmetry answer (cheap increments, no counterparty consent) was the debate's best reply but left the terminal step unexplained, which PRO exploited in closing.</best_rebuttal>
